The gloss of 'firstlings' as first-formed impulses and the identification of the figure as anaphora are both correct; the interpretation of this moment as Macbeth formally abandoning moral deliberation is the mainstream critical reading and is strongly supported by the surrounding action.

anchor_text: He wants the natural touch
summary: 'Wants' here means 'lacks,' not 'desires.' 'The natural touch' is the instinctive bond of love and protection that nature plants in a parent — the drive that makes even the smallest creature defend its young. Lady Macduff is saying Macduff has none of this instinct.
detail: The phrase draws on a commonplace of natural philosophy that all creatures, however weak, will fight to protect their offspring ('natural affection'). Shakespeare uses 'want' in the sense of 'lack' throughout the canon; it is one of the most common archaisms that trip modern readers. The contrast between 'natural touch' and Macduff's apparent indifference sets up the wren-and-owl image that follows: even the tiniest bird has what this man seems to lack.

anchor_text: The fits o' the season
summary: A 'fit' is a sudden violent seizure or episode — the same word used for an epileptic attack. 'The fits o' the season' means the sudden, violent upheavals of the present time: arrests, disappearances, and Macbeth's unpredictable rages. Ross is saying Macduff, as a wise man, understands these dangerous spasms better than most.

Applying the same word to the political situation implies that Macbeth's tyranny is itself a kind of mass seizure afflicting the whole kingdom — a body-politic metaphor consistent with the play's imagery of disease.

anchor_text: cruel are the times, when we are traitors, And do not know ourselves; when we hold rumour From what we fear
summary: Ross is describing a tyranny in which rumour and fear replace knowledge: people become 'traitors' without knowing why or how, accused on the strength of gossip. 'We hold rumour / From what we fear' means we cling to rumours generated by our own terror rather than by fact.
detail: The passage precisely captures the atmosphere of an informer-state in which denunciation is arbitrary and no one knows whose name has been given up next. For a Jacobean audience in 1606 the language would resonate with the aftermath of the Gunpowder Plot (November 1605): the months of arrests, interrogations, and executions that followed had exactly this quality of accusation spreading through association and rumour. The image of floating 'upon a wild and violent sea / Each way and move' — tossed without direction or anchor — condenses the terror of a subject who cannot predict which way the tyrant will turn. Ross's inability to say more ('I dare not speak much further') enacts the same silence that fear enforces.

anchor_text: the net nor lime, The pit-fall nor the gin
summary: All four are methods of trapping birds. A 'net' is a spread mesh snare; 'lime' is birdlime, a sticky substance smeared on twigs so birds land and cannot free their feet; a 'pit-fall' is a concealed hole or trap; a 'gin' is a spring-snare or noose. Lady Macduff is listing every method a fowler uses, saying the boy is too innocent to fear any of them — because he does not know such dangers exist.
detail: Birdlime (made from holly bark or mistletoe berries) was a standard and widely practised method of catching small birds in early modern England; it is the 'lime' that entangles in a dozen metaphors across Shakespeare (e.g., 'As lime does the bird's wings' in 3 Henry VI). The 'gin' as a spring-trap or noose appears frequently in hunting treatises of the period. The full catalogue reinforces the irony: the boy answers 'Why should I? Poor birds they are not set for' — he is so poor and unimportant that traps are not worth laying for him, precisely the innocence that cannot protect him from men who kill not for gain but by order.

anchor_text: one that swears and lies
summary: Lady Macduff defines a traitor as 'one that swears and lies' — someone who takes an oath and then breaks it. The boy immediately turns this into a paradox: since there are more liars and oath-breakers than honest men, the honest men would be outnumbered and hanged by the traitors. The exchange is a child's logic game that accidentally describes Scotland under Macbeth precisely: a world where the oath-breaker has seized power and 'honest men' are outnumbered.
detail: To 'swear and lie' means specifically to swear allegiance, loyalty, or an oath and then act contrary to it — the definitional act of a traitor in a monarchical legal framework. The boy's conclusion that 'the liars and swearers are fools' for not having hanged the honest men first is comic on its surface but devastatingly accurate about the political situation: Macbeth is indeed a man who swore fealty to Duncan and then murdered him, and he is not yet being hanged. The dialogue enacts the problem of a justice system overturned: when liars outnumber the honest, the law designed to hang traitors becomes inoperable. The wordplay on 'honest' — meaning both legally upright and numerically insufficient — sharpens the bitter joke.

anchor_text: I have done no harm. But I remember now I am in this earthly world; where to do harm Is often laudable; to do good sometime Accounted dangerous folly
summary: Lady Macduff starts to defend herself on the grounds that she is innocent — then catches herself. She knows that in Macbeth's Scotland innocence is not a protection: doing harm is rewarded, and doing good is 'accounted dangerous folly.' The speech is a precise moral diagnosis of a tyrant's state, where virtue and safety have been completely severed.
detail: The passage inverts the moral world: good and evil have exchanged their expected consequences, just as 'fair is foul, and foul is fair' in the witches' opening chant. Lady Macduff's recognition comes too late — the murderers are already at the door — but it crystallises the play's central concern with the corruption of moral order under tyranny. The rhetorical structure is chiasmus (harm praised / good condemned), which formally mirrors the world turned upside down. The 'womanly defence' she rejects is the claim of innocence: in a lawless state, innocence is merely a vulnerability, not a shield. The speech also implicitly indicts her absent husband: to be safe in such a world, he has done what might be accounted good — fled to oppose the tyrant — but has left her with no defence at all.

anchor_text: in no place so unsanctified Where such as thou mayst find him
summary: 'Unsanctified' means not made holy, not consecrated — a place with no claim to God's protection. Lady Macduff hopes Macduff is somewhere sacred enough that murderers like this one cannot enter it. The line conveys both her contempt for the murderer and her faith that there are still places beyond the reach of Macbeth's violence.
detail: The word choice is pointed: 'unsanctified' is the category the murderers themselves inhabit. In a play permeated by the language of sacred and profane — Duncan's murder as a desecration, Macbeth's castle as a hell, the English court as a place where the King heals by touch — Lady Macduff's last words before the killing frames the scene as a violation of sanctuary. The phrase also echoes Lady Macbeth's earlier invocation of spirits to 'unsex' her and 'stop up the access and passage to remorse' — the systematic unsanctifying of persons that Macbeth's regime enacts.

anchor_text: thou shag-haar'd villain
summary: 'Shag-haired' means rough-haired or shaggy — the boy hurls the insult at a man with wild, unkempt hair, the visual marker of a hired ruffian or a villain from the lower orders. 'Young fry of treachery' (the murderer's answering taunt) means 'small fry' — the spawn or offspring of a traitor, using the word for fish-spawn ('fry') to imply the boy is small, worthless, and insignificant.
detail: Both insults are precise about social rank: 'shag-haired' codes the murderer as a rough-looking low-life, not a gentleman; 'fry' (young fish, or the spawn of fish) reduces the boy to something tiny and disposable, denying him any human weight. The exchange is the play's most brutal compression: a child's brave, futile insult answered by a murder. 'Haar'd' is a Scots spelling variant ('haar' = shaggy hair); some editors modernise to 'shag-haired.' The courage of Macduff's son — defending his absent father to the last — contrasts pointedly with the murderer's cowardice in killing a child.

summary: 'Birthdom' is an archaic word for one's native country — literally 'the realm into which one was born.' To 'bestride' something fallen means to stand astride it defensively, as a soldier straddles a fallen comrade to protect him. Macduff urges Malcolm to stand over Scotland like a protector rather than weep over it.

anchor_text: Strike heaven on the face, that it resounds

The phrase 'like syllable of dolour' means an exact answering sound of sorrow, as if heaven repeats the cry word for word. The register is high prophetic complaint, drawing on the Psalms tradition of outcry to God.

anchor_text: He has no children

summary: A 'kite' was a common scavenging bird of prey, seen daily above London streets feeding on offal and waste; it was a byword for low predatory rapacity. A 'hell-kite' is a kite from hell — a devil in bird form. Macduff casts Macbeth as a swooping predator who has taken his whole brood of 'chickens' (children) and their 'dam' (mother) in 'one fell swoop' — one sudden, savage strike. 'Fell' means fierce, savage.
detail: Kites were so numerous above Elizabethan London that they are cited in travel accounts as a characteristic feature of the city. They were scavengers and occasional thieves, known to swoop at children and small animals. The falconry vocabulary ('swoop') combined with the hell-kite image makes Macbeth a diabolical predator rather than a tragic figure — the imagery shifts toward pure condemnation. 'Dame' (here 'dam') means mother in both the animal (brood-mother) and human sense.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'kite' n.1, sense 1: 'a bird of prey of the hawk family'; sense 3: 'a rapacious or predatory person'; OED s.v. 'fell' adj.1: 'fierce, savage, cruel.'

The cultural context of kites as common scavengers above London, their use as a byword for predatory rapacity, and 'fell' as savage are all accurate; the extension to the broader predator-imagery of the closing passage is a defensible structural observation.

anchor_text: Did heaven look on, / And would not take their part? Sinful Macduff, / They were all struck for thee
summary: Macduff blames himself for his family's deaths: because he sinned and fled without protecting them, God allowed them to be killed as punishment for him, not for anything they had done. The theology is the Old Testament pattern of collective punishment — the sins of the father visited on his household — which runs through Exodus 20:5 and is widely invoked in tragedy to explain innocent suffering.
detail: The idea that God punishes a man's household for his sins echoes Exodus 20:5 ('visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children') and shapes much of the suffering in the Old Testament histories. Macduff does not question God's justice; he accepts that his own guilt caused his family's death, and that God simply watched it happen. The guilt here is not for his flight (which the play frames as right) but for leaving them unguarded — the 'rawness' Malcolm named earlier. The self-accusation is emotionally devastating precisely because it is theologically coherent within the period's framework.

sources.citation: Exodus 20:5 (Geneva 1599): 'visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation'; compare Numbers 32:23.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1938

Exodus 20:5 Geneva 1599 'visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation' is a real verse that accurately supports the collective-punishment theology described.

The collective-punishment theology drawn from Exodus 20:5 is the correct Old Testament parallel; the reading that Macduff blames himself while accepting divine justice is consistent with the text and theologically coherent within a Protestant 1606 frame.

anchor_text: Macbeth / Is ripe for shaking, and the powers above / Put on their instruments
summary: Malcolm frames the coming campaign against Macbeth as a divine mission: 'the powers above' (God and the angels) are arming themselves, and Malcolm's army is their instrument. 'Put on their instruments' means to arm or equip their human agents. The language of providential war — God working through earthly soldiers — places the assault on a tyrant in the same frame as the great-chain-of-being doctrine that regicide disorders creation.
detail: The metaphor casts the army as weapons in God's hands, not free agents. The same providential framing appears in the English histories (Henry V at Agincourt) and in the Holinshed-sourced tragedies, where legitimate rulers who have been displaced are ultimately restored by an order that transcends the merely political. 'Ripe for shaking' develops the earlier agricultural metaphors in the scene and implies that Macbeth's tyranny has now reached its appointed end — like an overripe fruit ready to fall.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Compare Romans 13:1-4 (Geneva 1599): the 'powers' as God's ordained instruments of justice; see also Psalms 82 on divine judgment against tyrants.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1953
Romans 13:1-4 (powers as God's ordained instruments of justice) and Psalms 82 (divine judgment against tyrants) are real Geneva Bible texts that support the providential-war framing described.

The providential war framing ('God arming human agents') is correctly identified as the dominant register; 'ripe for shaking' as overripe fruit ready to fall is a standard gloss and does not overreach.

anchor_text: A great perturbation in nature,--to receive at once the benefit of sleep
summary: The Doctor means that sleepwalking is a serious disorder of nature: Lady Macbeth enjoys the body of sleep yet performs the acts of waking ('the effects of watching'). 'Perturbation' here carries its medical sense of a violent disturbance or upset of the body's natural order.
detail: Early modern physicians understood health as a balance of the four humours; any condition that blurred the boundary between sleep and waking — a state in which reason was supposed to be fully suspended — counted as a grave 'perturbation.' 'Slumbery agitation' (line 1966) compounds the paradox: the Latin-derived 'slumbery' (drowsy, sleeping) is set against the vigorous 'agitation' (restless movement). The Doctor's clinical framing will give way by the scene's end to his frank admission that the case is beyond medicine.

The medical/humoral gloss on 'perturbation' and the paradox of 'slumbery agitation' are both standard early modern readings with no over-reach.

anchor_text: seem thus washing her hands: I have known her continue in this a quarter of an hour
summary: Lady Macbeth's compulsive, unconscious hand-washing enacts the opposite of her earlier confidence that 'a little water clears us of this deed' (2.1). The gesture echoes Pontius Pilate, who washed his hands before the crowd to claim innocence in the death of Jesus — the biblical image of a public washing that cannot actually cleanse blood-guilt.
detail: In Matthew 27:24 Pilate 'tooke water, and washed his handes before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just man' — a ritual that left him morally responsible nonetheless. Lady Macbeth had wielded exactly this logic: physical cleansing equals moral release. Her sleepwalking now shows that her own unconscious mind has rejected it. The reference-card on Pilate notes the same futility; it was already anticipated in Richard II, but Macbeth makes the hand-washing its central, recurring image of failed expiation.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 27:24 (Geneva 1599): Pilate washes his hands before the multitude, disclaiming responsibility for the blood of Jesus.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1980

Geneva Bible 1599 Matthew 27:24 confirmed: 'he tooke water and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this iust man,' matching the annotation's paraphrase exactly.

The hand-washing in 5.1 is most directly an inversion of Lady Macbeth's own earlier line ('a little water clears us of this deed,' 2.2), and calling the Pilate parallel the primary or 'central' image elevates a possible resonance above the stronger internal echo; the allusion is plausible but not demonstrably intended by the text of this scene.

anchor_text: Out, damned spot! out, I say!-- One; two; why, then 'tis time to do't
summary: The 'One; two' counts the strokes of the clock — Lady Macbeth is reliving the night of Duncan's murder, when she awaited the signal bell (2.1). 'Damned spot' addresses the imagined bloodstain on her hand: 'spot' was a common word for a moral blemish or stain as well as a physical mark, and 'damned' means cursed or hellish.
detail: In 2.1 Lady Macbeth set out a drugged posset for the grooms, struck a bell as Macbeth's signal to murder, and afterward steadied him: 'A little water clears us of this deed.' Now, in sleep, she is back in that moment — the clock-strokes, the command to act — but the reassurance has collapsed into horror. 'Damned' modifies the stain with its theological force: the spot is not merely dirty but damnation-marked. The repetition of 'out' enacts futile effort against something that will not go.

sources.name: Onions

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'damned': 'cursed, infernal, accursed.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1985
Onions s.v. 'spot' (moral taint) and Schmidt s.v. 'damned' (cursed, infernal) are standard, accurate lexicographical sources that directly support the vocabulary claims made.
The clock-count reading, the gloss on 'spot' as moral blemish, and the reliving-of-2.1 interpretation are all mainstream and textually grounded.

anchor_text: The Thane of Fife had a wife; where is she now?
summary: The Thane of Fife is Macduff, who fled to England, leaving his wife and children behind. In Act 4 Scene 2 Macbeth's murderers slaughtered them in their castle. Lady Macbeth's question — 'where is she now?' — reveals that she knows about this atrocity, and that it is part of the guilt unraveling her.
detail: A thane was a Scottish nobleman, roughly equivalent to an English earl; Fife is a region of eastern Scotland, and Macduff held it. His flight to join Malcolm was the provocation Macbeth chose to punish by killing the Macduff family. The jingle-like rhyme ('Fife...wife') has the quality of something Lady Macbeth may have repeated to herself, perhaps a phrase overheard or a bit of court gossip, now surfacing in her unconscious alongside Duncan's murder. It exposes the breadth of her complicity: she is not haunted only by Duncan but by the cascade of violence his murder set off.

The identification of Macduff and the reading that the murder of Lady Macduff surfaces here in guilt-association are standard critical interpretations supported by the play's own action in 4.2.

anchor_text: all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand
summary: Arabia was proverbially the source of the costliest perfumes and spices in Shakespeare's world — frankincense, myrrh, and aloeswood came overland through Arabian trading routes. Lady Macbeth invokes the most extravagant imagined quantity of sweetness to say it would still be insufficient: the blood-smell she senses (though no one else can) is beyond any physical remedy.
detail: The Arabian spice trade was the great luxury commerce of the ancient and medieval worlds; the region's name carried an almost mythical association with overwhelming fragrance, and Pliny records the vast sums Rome spent on its aromatics. The hyperbole inverts the earlier logic of the murder night: then she insisted that a little water would clean everything; now the entirety of the world's perfumes would not. The contrast marks the full collapse of her rationalist courage. Her moan — 'Oh, oh, oh!' (TLN 1998) — is the Doctor's cue to remark that 'the heart is sorely charged': oppressed, loaded with grief and guilt.

sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 12 (chs. 30-35: 'the country of frankincense,' frankincense and myrrh): Arabia ('Arabia Felix') as the source of the ancient world's costliest aromatics and the centre of the spice trade.

anchor_text: More needs she the divine than the physician
summary: The Doctor concludes that Lady Macbeth's illness is beyond medicine: what she needs is a divine — a clergyman or confessor — not a doctor. In Elizabethan understanding, diseases rooted in guilt and sin were spiritual, not bodily, and only religious absolution could address them.
detail: Early modern medicine drew a firm line between bodily complaints, which the physician could treat, and spiritual sickness — guilt, melancholy arising from a troubled conscience, despair — which belonged to the divine (priest or minister). The Doctor's verdict is a diagnosis of conscience-disease: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking and compulsive hand-washing are symptoms not of a physical disorder but of guilt that only God can absolve. His final couplet — 'I think, but dare not speak' (TLN 2024) — shows his awareness that to speak plainly of what he has seen and heard would be dangerous in Macbeth's Scotland.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'divine' n. 2b: 'a clergyman, minister of religion; one skilled in divinity.'

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'divine' n.: 'a clergyman, divine; one who tends to the soul as the physician does to the body.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2019

OED s.v. 'divine' n. 2b and Schmidt both confirm the word meant 'clergyman' in early modern English; the cultural claim about physician vs. divine roles is well-supported by these lexical sources and general early modern medical history.
The early modern physician/divine distinction is well-documented, and the reading of the Doctor's self-silencing as political fear in a tyranny is a defensible and standard interpretation.

anchor_text: My mind she has mated, and amaz'd my sight
summary: 'Mated' here does not mean paired or married — it is a chess term meaning checkmated: defeated, confounded, brought to a standstill. The Doctor says Lady Macbeth's words and actions have left his mind completely at a loss. 'Amaz'd' reinforces this: in early modern English it meant bewildered or stunned into inaction, not merely surprised.
detail: 'To mate' in the sense of to checkmate, stupefy, or overpower with astonishment appears in several Shakespeare plays (e.g., Comedy of Errors 3.2: 'I am mated'). Together with 'amaz'd' — which retains its older force of 'struck into a maze, utterly confused' — the Doctor's couplet marks the limit of rational understanding: what he has witnessed cannot be processed within the categories available to a physician. His self-silencing ('I think, but dare not speak') then adds political fear: the Scotland outside these walls is a tyrant's kingdom.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mate' v.2: 'to checkmate; to put in a helpless position; to confuse utterly' — from Old French mat (defeated).

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mated': 'confounded, stupefied, helpless as a king in check.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2023

OED s.v. 'mate' v.2 (to checkmate; confuse utterly, from Old French mat) and Onions s.v. 'mated' (confounded, helpless as a king in check) are accurate and directly support the chess-term etymology claimed.
The chess-term etymology for 'mated' and the older force of 'amaz'd' as 'driven into a maze of confusion' are both accurate and well-attested in early modern usage.

anchor_text: Revenges burn in them; for their dear causes Would to the bleeding and the grim alarm Excite the mortified man.
summary: 'Mortified' here means made dead or deadened — spiritually numbed, drained of all feeling. Menteith says that even a man reduced to utter numbness (the mortified man, as dead inside as if already in the grave) would be roused to fight by these causes. The word comes from Latin mortificare, 'to cause to die'; it also carries a religious sense of one who has killed off worldly feeling through penance — making the image even more extreme.
detail: In Elizabethan usage 'mortified' covered three overlapping senses: (1) physically deadened or gangrenous (flesh that has 'died' before the body); (2) spiritually disciplined to the point of insensibility, as in the language of ascetic devotion; and (3) simply struck dead. All three senses intensify the rhetoric here: the outrage is so live that it would galvanize even a man utterly beyond feeling. Holinshed's account of the thanes rallying against Macbeth underlies the passage; Shakespeare amplifies it with this physiological-spiritual extremity. Compare Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here' appeal to spirits to 'stop up the access and passage to remorse' — a voluntary mortification that she comes to regret.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mortified' adj., senses 1 (killed, deadened) and 2 (subdued by self-denial); first cited use of sense 1 predates Shakespeare.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'mortified': 'killed, deadened, having lost sensation.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2028

OED senses for 'mortified' (killed/deadened; subdued by self-denial) and Latin etymology mortificare are well-attested; Schmidt s.v. 'mortified' as 'killed, deadened, having lost sensation' is consistent with the standard lexicographic record.

Both primary senses of 'mortified' (physically deadened; ascetically numbed) are well-attested Elizabethan usage, and the rhetorical logic — even the utterly insensible man would be roused — is clear in the text; the Lady Macbeth comparison in the detail is a slight stretch but does not corrupt the core gloss.

anchor_text: I have a file Of all the gentry: there is Siward's son And many unrough youths, that even now Protest their first of manhood.
summary: A 'file' here is a list or roll-call — a written catalogue of names, the sense from which 'filing' a document derives. 'Unrough' means unbearded, too young to have grown a beard (rough = bearded or hairy). 'Protest their first of manhood' means publicly demonstrate for the first time that they are men — young soldiers earning their spurs in this campaign. Lennox is reporting that the army includes not just seasoned nobles but boys making their first appearance as fighting men.
detail: In 3.1 Macbeth himself uses 'file' in the same sense when he asks the murderers if they can find themselves 'in the catalogue ye go for men' — a list or register. 'Unrough' is a rare coinage (this is its only use in Shakespeare); it vividly pictures callow recruits. The detail matters dramatically: the rebels' army is young and idealistic, while Macbeth grows isolated and commands only through fear ('Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love' — 2047-2048). The combination of Siward's son (who will die bravely in 5.7) and these beardless youths prepares for the final battle's mixture of chivalry and recklessness.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'file' n., sense 9: 'a list, roll, catalogue of persons'; and s.v. 'unrough' adj.: 'not yet rough (bearded)' — first attested here.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'file': 'list, enumeration' and s.v. 'unrough': 'beardless, juvenile.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2034

OED 'file' n. as 'list, roll, catalogue' is a genuine sense; Onions confirms 'file' as 'list or roll' and 'unrough' as 'smooth, beardless' (first attested in Shakespeare per Onions), supporting both the word glosses and the hapax claim.

'File' as list/roll-call is well-attested and paralleled at 3.1, 'unrough' as beardless is the only defensible gloss, and 'protest their first of manhood' as a first public demonstration of martial manhood is the standard reading with no overreach.

anchor_text: cannot buckle his distemper'd cause Within the belt of rule
summary: Caithness and Angus use a sustained clothing metaphor to describe Macbeth's failed kingship. 'Distemper'd' means diseased or disordered (a 'distemper' is an illness); he cannot buckle — fasten with a belt — his swollen, diseased cause within the rule of law. The metaphor runs on: he feels his stolen title 'hang loose about him, like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.' A king's role is an office that must fit the man who holds it. Macbeth the usurper wears authority like a garment made for someone else.
detail: The clothing metaphor is one of the play's controlling images from the start ('Why do you dress me in borrowed robes?' — 1.3; 'new honours come upon him, / Like our strange garments,' — 1.3). Here it reaches its most explicit statement: legitimate kingship is a garment proportioned to the wearer, and Macbeth is a small thief trying to wear a giant's cloak. 'Distemper'd' adds the medical register that runs through Act 5 (the Doctor, Lady Macbeth's sick mind, the 'sickly weal' two lines later). 'Belt of rule' puns on the legal sense of 'rule' (governance, law) and the physical belt that holds a garment to the body: Macbeth's cause cannot contain itself, it overflows, bulges, refuses to stay in its proper bounds. The passage also draws on the doctrine of the king's two bodies: the body politic (the office) should clothe the body natural (the man) only when that man is the rightful king.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd edn (1587), Scottish history — the basis for the political collapse around Macbeth in Act 5.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'distemper'd': 'diseased, disturbed, out of order.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2042

Holinshed (1587) legitimately underlies the political collapse context in Act 5 even though the clothing/belt metaphor is Shakespeare's own invention; Schmidt's gloss of 'distemper'd' as 'diseased, disturbed, out of order' is corroborated by Onions, and both cited sources support the claims made of them.

The clothing metaphor as a controlling image across the play is mainstream critical consensus (Spurgeon, Cleanth Brooks), not a Romantic-era invention; 'distemper'd' carrying both medical and disorder senses is accurate, and the giant's-robe extension (TLN 2049-2050, Angus) is correctly identified as part of the same metaphorical cluster even though it belongs to a different speaker than the anchor lines.

anchor_text: Now minutely revolts upbraid his faith-breach
summary: 'Minutely' means 'at every minute' — continuously, without pause. 'Faith-breach' is Angus's coinage for Macbeth's treachery, literally a breaking of faith. The line says that rebellions happening every minute of the day rebuke Macbeth for being the original oath-breaker.
detail: The adverb 'minutely' is rare and precise: it does not mean 'in small detail' (its modern sense) but 'every minute, incessant.' The neologism 'faith-breach' — not found elsewhere in Shakespeare — packs the moral charge of the scene into a single compound: Macbeth who murdered his guest and king was the supreme faith-breaker, and those now defecting merely imitate, on a smaller scale, the treachery he modelled. The irony is that his original crime is now being mirrored back at him by his own subjects. The passage belongs to the scene's running imagery of physical sickness and moral disorder — Macbeth's 'distemper'd cause' cannot be contained, and the upbraid (public reproach) is incessant.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'minutely' adv.: 'every minute, incessantly'; the Macbeth passage is the only cited example.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'minutely': 'occurring every minute.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2046

Onions confirmed via Perseus as '(not pre-S.): happening every minute,' citing Mac 5.2.18, which supports both the adverbial gloss and the implication of Shakespearean coinage; the OED 'only cited example' description is consistent with Onions calling it not pre-Shakespearean.

'Minutely' as 'every minute / incessantly' is the only grammatically coherent reading (the modern 'in small detail' sense would be anachronistic and syntactically awkward with 'revolts'), and the irony that Macbeth's own treachery is now mirrored back by defecting subjects is straightforwardly present in the text.

anchor_text: medicine of the sickly weal; And with him pour we, in our country's purge, Each drop of us
summary: Caithness and Lennox cast Malcolm as a physician and Scotland as a diseased patient. 'Weal' means 'commonwealth' or 'welfare' (as in the old phrase 'the common weal'). A 'purge' was a medical dose to cleanse the body of corrupt matter. The lords offer themselves as medicine — each drop of their blood a drop of the cure — to flush out Macbeth's tyranny. Lennox extends the metaphor: they will 'dew' (moisten, nourish) Malcolm, 'the sovereign flower,' and drown the weeds — where 'sovereign' means both 'royal' and, in medical usage, 'supremely effective as a remedy.'
detail: The medical language of Act 5 is systematic. The Doctor in 5.1 confesses Lady Macbeth's disease is beyond his art; Macbeth in 5.3 demands of the Doctor a cure for Scotland's sickness ('What rhubarb, cyme, or what purgative drug / Would scour these English hence?'); and here the rebels speak of the whole nation as a body requiring medicine. 'Purge' was a standard early modern medical and political term: to purge the body politic of corrupt humours was a familiar analogy for removing a tyrant. 'Sovereign' captures both senses exactly — a sovereign remedy was one of absolute efficacy (OED s.v. 'sovereign' adj. 2), so 'sovereign flower' means at once the true king and the supremely healing plant. The gardening imagery (flower versus weeds) echoes the garden-of-state metaphors of Shakespeare's histories — a good king is the sovereign garden plant; a tyrant is an overgrown weed that chokes the rest.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sovereign' adj., sense 2: 'potent or efficacious above all others; of supreme efficacy' (medical); and sense 1: 'supreme in rank, of a ruler.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'weal': 'state, commonwealth, welfare of the state.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2057

OED 'sovereign' adj. sense 2 (supremely efficacious as a remedy) is a real and well-documented sense; Onions s.v. 'weal' confirmed via Perseus as covering 'welfare' and 'commonwealth,' which adequately supports the annotation's gloss.

All three lexical readings are sound — 'weal' as commonwealth, 'purge' as medical/political purgative, and 'sovereign' as a deliberate pun on royal authority and supreme medicinal efficacy — and the garden-of-state flower/weed extension at TLN 2061 is borne out by Lennox's exact words.

anchor_text: Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane
summary: Macbeth quotes back the Third Apparition's prophecy verbatim (4.1): he will not be defeated 'until Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill shall come against him.' Since forests do not move, he treats it as an absolute guarantee of safety. The audience knows, from 5.4, that Malcolm's soldiers will cut branches from Birnam wood to use as camouflage — making the prophecy literally true while defeating Macbeth.
detail: This is the play's central example of the witches' 'equivocation': each prophecy is technically true but engineered to mislead. The Third Apparition (a crowned child holding a tree) delivered the prophecy at TLN 1681-1686. Macbeth's bravado here is built on a misreading: he hears 'impossible condition' where the witches meant 'disguised soldiers carrying boughs.' See also the second prophecy ('none of woman born') reprised in the next lines.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Holinshed, Raphael. The Third Volume of Chronicles. London, 1587. 'Macbeth' section: Macbeth fortifies Dunsinane and trusts the oracles; Malcolm's men cut branches at Birnam.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2064

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does describe Macbeth trusting the prophecies while fortifying Dunsinane, and Malcolm's soldiers cutting branches from Birnam Wood as camouflage — the source directly supports the summary claims.

The equivocation reading of the Birnam wood prophecy is the mainstream scholarly consensus, the 4.1 citation is accurate, and the summary correctly anticipates the literal fulfillment in 5.4 without over-reading.

anchor_text: mingle with the English epicures
summary: 'Epicures' is a slur meaning pleasure-seekers and self-indulgents, not philosophers. Macbeth uses it to dismiss the Scottish thanes who have defected to Malcolm's English-backed army as soft, luxury-loving Southerners who have abandoned Scottish martial hardness. The insult carries a stock Jacobean-era contrast between tough Scots and supposedly pampered English courtiers.
detail: 'Epicure' derives from the Greek philosopher Epicurus (341-270 BCE), whose followers were popularly (and inaccurately) caricatured as devoted to physical pleasure. By Shakespeare's time the word had become a general English term of contempt for a voluptuary or glutton: OED s.v. 'epicure' sense 2 records this pejorative usage from the 16th century onward. The contempt also carries political edge: Malcolm is sheltered at the English court of Edward the Confessor (4.3), so 'English epicures' indirectly insults King Edward's nation.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'epicure', sense 2: 'One who gives himself up to sensual pleasure; a glutton, sybarite' (usage from 1560s).

anchor_text: lily-liver'd boy
summary: Macbeth's rapid sequence of insults — 'lily-liver'd', 'linen cheeks', 'whey-face', 'cream-fac'd' — all attack the servant's pallor as proof of cowardice. In early modern physiology, the liver was the seat of courage; a 'lily-livered' man was thought to have a white (bloodless) liver, meaning no bravery. Pale cheeks and a white face confirmed the same verdict: fear had drained the blood.
detail: Early modern medicine held that the liver produced blood, which in turn generated the heat and 'spirit' of courage. A brave man's liver ran red; a coward's ran pale or white. 'Linen' (undyed white cloth), 'lily', 'cream', and 'whey' (the watery part of curdled milk) are all white — Macbeth piles up the synonyms to mock and shame. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'lily-livered': 'white-livered, cowardly' with this line as the citation. The cluster also foreshadows the scene's irony: Macbeth himself is masking his own fear behind aggression.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. A Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'lily-livered': 'white-livered, cowardly.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'liver': 'considered as the seat of courage, love, or passion.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2079

The Onions Shakespeare Glossary entry for 'lily-livered' ('white-livered, cowardly') is confirmed on Perseus with this Macbeth line as the citation, and Schmidt's entry for 'liver' as the seat of courage is a real and well-known entry.

The humoral physiology behind 'lily-livered' is standard early modern medicine, and the dramatic irony reading — that Macbeth's aggression masks his own fear — is defensible given his 'I am sick at heart' admission in the same scene (TLN 2084).

anchor_text: cast the water of my land, find her disease
summary: 'Cast the water' is the standard early modern phrase for diagnosing illness by examining a urine sample. Macbeth pivots from asking the Doctor to cure Lady Macbeth to asking him to diagnose and purge Scotland itself of the English army — as if the country were a sick patient whose urine could be inspected. The metaphor collapses the personal and political: Scotland and Lady Macbeth share the same disease, guilt-driven disorder.
detail: Uroscopy — examining the color, smell, sediment, and clarity of urine — was the dominant diagnostic tool of early modern medicine; a physician 'casting water' could supposedly identify the humor imbalance causing illness. The conceit of Scotland as a sick body is conventional in political thought (cf. the body-politic metaphor in 'Coriolanus' 1.1), but here Macbeth also means it literally: 'What rhubarb, senna, or what purgative drug / Would scour these English hence?' (TLN 2125-2126) — rhubarb root and senna were standard laxative purgatives used to expel excess humor. The cure Macbeth fantasizes is purging an invading army as if it were bad blood.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'water' (cast the water): 'to examine the urine as a medical diagnosis.'

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2120

The uroscopy gloss is accurate, the body-politic parallel to Coriolanus 1.1 is a legitimate comparative note, and the reading that Scotland and Lady Macbeth share the same guilt-driven disorder is directly supported by the scene's juxtaposition.

anchor_text: What rhubarb, senna, or what purgative drug
summary: Rhubarb root (from Rheum species, imported via Turkey from Central Asia) and senna (a pod-bearing shrub from Africa and Asia) were the two most common laxative purgatives in early modern English pharmacy, used to 'scour' the bowels of excess humor. Macbeth uses them as a darkly comic shorthand: if Scotland is a sick body, what medicine will purge the English invaders as a physician would purge bad matter from the gut?

anchor_text: hew him down a bough, And bear't before him
summary: Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a bough from Birnam Wood and carry it as camouflage, so that scouts will miscount the army. The order unwittingly begins to fulfill the Third Apparition's promise that Macbeth 'shall never vanquish'd be until / Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill / shall come against him' (4.1). The prophecy seemed to guarantee safety because a forest cannot move; it is undone by a battlefield ruse that Macbeth never imagined.
detail: The wood-bough stratagem comes directly from Holinshed's Chronicles (1587), History of Scotland: Malcolm's forces 'cut down branches from trees to bear before them' to hide their numbers. Shakespeare keeps the detail but invests it with the dramatic irony of the prophecy: the audience, who heard the Third Apparition speak, watches the fulfillment begin while Macbeth remains ignorant. This is the play's central instance of the theme announced by the Porter and stated outright by Macbeth at 5.5: 'the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth.' The witches' prophecy was literally true -- a wood does come against Dunsinane -- but in a sense that defeats rather than protects. The same equivocating logic destroys the other assurance: Macduff was 'not of woman born' in any ordinary sense (5.8).

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd ed. (1587), History of Scotland: Malcolm's forces bear boughs to disguise their numbers on the march to Dunsinane.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2139

Holinshed 1587 History of Scotland confirms the bough-camouflage detail verbatim: 'he commanded euerie man to get a bough of some trée or other of that wood in his hand... and to march foorth therewith in such wise, that on the next morrow they might come closelie and without sight'; the annotation's paraphrase is accurate.

The Holinshed source, the dramatic-irony reading of the prophecy's fulfillment, and the equivocation theme are all mainstream and textually grounded; the detail's reference to the Porter is slightly loose (the Porter scene targets Jesuit equivocation specifically), but the equivocation-of-the-fiend link to 5.5 is direct and the overall interpretation is sound.

anchor_text: Both more and less have given him the revolt
summary: 'More and less' is an Elizabethan idiom for 'greater and lesser' -- that is, noblemen and commoners alike. Malcolm is saying that Macbeth's support has collapsed at every rank of society: both the great lords and the ordinary soldiers have defected from him.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, 2nd ed. (Oxford, 1919), s.v. 'more': 'more and less = great and small, persons of all ranks.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2149

Onions' Shakespeare Glossary is a real work and 'more and less' meaning persons of all ranks is well attested in Shakespeare (cf. Henry IV Part 1), but the exact quoted wording attributed to Onions ('more and less = great and small, persons of all ranks') cannot be verified from available text of the entry, and Onions typically phrases such entries differently; the source is real but the precise quotation is unconfirmable.
'More and less' meaning persons of all ranks (great and small) is well-documented Elizabethan usage and fits the line's plain sense without over-reading.

anchor_text: Let our just censures Attend the true event
summary: 'Censures' here means 'judgments' or 'assessments,' not blame. Macduff is urging the leaders to hold back their evaluations of the situation until the battle has actually told them what is true. The caution is pointed: the last three scenes have been full of intelligence reports about Macbeth's position, none of them fully reliable.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2152

OED sense of 'censure' as 'judgment, opinion' (without negative connotation) is well established, and the Hamlet 1.3 example ('Take each man's censure, but reserve thy judgment') is confirmed exactly by the MIT Shakespeare text.

'Censures' in the neutral sense of 'judgments' is standard Elizabethan usage, the Hamlet parallel is genuine, and Macduff's caution about premature assessment is a straightforward reading of the line.

anchor_text: Thoughts speculative their unsure hopes relate; But certain issue strokes must arbitrate
summary: Siward closes the scene with a sententia -- a compressed, aphoristic maxim of the kind common in Senecan drama and rhetoric: speculation can only report uncertain hopes, but the real outcome will be decided by blows. 'Arbitrate' means 'decide' or 'settle' (as an arbitrator settles a dispute). The couplet is a soldier's blunt dismissal of all the political talk above it: words and guesses have their limit; the fighting will tell.
detail: The sententia (Latin for 'maxim') was a favored closing device in Roman tragedy, especially Seneca, and in English rhetorical training deriving from it. Siward's couplet is structurally chiastic -- uncertain thought versus certain action, the verb 'relate' (merely report) versus 'arbitrate' (decide) -- and it performs what it describes, shutting down deliberation and moving the army forward. 'Speculative' in early modern usage means 'pertaining to speculation or conjecture' rather than the modern sense of financial risk; OED records it from the sixteenth century. The speech functions dramatically to close the scene on a note of martial decisiveness that is immediately undercut by what the audience knows: the 'certain issue' will include Young Siward's death.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'speculative' adj. 2: 'of the nature of conjecture or hypothesis' (in use from 1590s); s.v. 'arbitrate' v. 2: 'to decide, determine, settle' (Shakespeare, c. 1600-1610).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2158

OED records 'speculative' in the conjecture/hypothesis sense from the 1570s onward and 'arbitrate' as 'to decide or settle' in Shakespeare-era usage; the sententia as a Senecan closing device in Elizabethan drama is confirmed by multiple scholarly sources, and the couplet's function as described is accurate.

Identifying the closing couplet as a sententia in the Senecan tradition is mainstream, the word-sense glosses for 'speculative' and 'arbitrate' are correct, and the dramatic-irony note about Young Siward is defensible; the label 'chiastic' is imprecise (the structure is contrastive-parallel rather than A-B/B-A inversion), but this is a minor rhetorical over-precision that does not undermine the reading.

anchor_text: famine and the ague eat them up
summary: 'Ague' is a violent fever — typically the recurring chills and sweats of malaria, then endemic in parts of Britain — used broadly for any wasting fever. Macbeth is saying the besieging army will rot outside his walls from hunger and disease before they can take the castle.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ague' n. 1: 'An acute fever, usually malarial in origin, attended by recurring fits of chills and sweating.' Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'ague': 'intermittent fever, malaria.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2164
OED s.v. 'ague' n.1 and Onions Shakespeare Glossary are real, standard references whose definitions (recurring malarial fever with chills and sweating) directly support the summary claim.
Standard archaic-vocab gloss: 'ague' as malarial/intermittent fever is uncontested, and the reading of Macbeth's contemptuous boast about the siege is accurate to the text.

anchor_text: my fell of hair / Would at a dismal treatise rouse and stir
summary: 'Fell' here means a hide or pelt of hair — the whole fleece on one's head and body. 'Dismal treatise' is a terrifying tale or account ('dismal' from medieval Latin 'dies mali,' unlucky days; 'treatise' used loosely for any narrative). Macbeth is recalling a time when a horrible story would make every hair on his body stand on end.
detail: The phrase 'fell of hair' (or 'pell') appears in F1 as 'fell'; editors have occasionally emended to 'feel,' but the 'pelt / fleece' reading is well supported and more vivid. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fell' sb.2: 'the skin with the hair, a fleece.' The image of hair rising in horror ('as life were in't') belongs to the classical and early-modern physiology of fear, in which the animal spirits contract and make hairs erect.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fell' sb.2: 'the skin, hide, with the hair on it; a fleece.' OED s.v. 'fell' n.2: 'the skin or hide of an animal, especially with the wool or hair on it; a pelt.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2172

Schmidt Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'fell' sb.2 and OED s.v. 'fell' n.2 are real references whose definitions ('skin with the hair on it; a pelt') accurately support the 'pelt/fleece' reading of the anchor text.
'Fell' as hide or pelt is the mainstream F1 reading, correctly distinguished from the 'feel' emendation; the fear-physiology detail is period-accurate and the gloss does not over-reach.

anchor_text: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, / Creeps in this petty pace from day to day
summary: Macbeth's soliloquy on hearing of Lady Macbeth's death uses two interlocking rhetorical figures. The triple 'To-morrow' is anaphora — the same word hammered at the start of three phrases — to make time feel grinding and mechanical. It then extends into a sustained metaphor: life is an actor ('a poor player') who struts and frets through one hour on the stage, then is heard no more; and a 'tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.' The point is that all the noise and action of a human life add up to nothing, spoken on his wife's death.
detail: The theatrical conceit is central. In Elizabethan usage a 'player' is an actor; to 'strut and fret' is to perform with exaggerated gesture and emotion for a single turn on stage ('his hour upon the stage'), then fall silent forever. 'Sound and fury' renders the play's noise as mere theatrical spectacle without meaning. The anaphora ('To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow') mimics the relentless tick of days while 'creeps in this petty pace' slows the rhythm to a crawl — a contrast between the word's repetition and the deadening drag of time. The soliloquy is Macbeth's most complete philosophical statement: by this point he has lost the very things his crimes were meant to secure, and the speech converts his grief into nihilism. The de casibus pattern — a prince brought from greatness to ruin — is reinterpreted here not as Fortune's turning but as the meaninglessness of ambition itself.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'player' n. 3a: 'One who acts in a play; an actor.' Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fret' v.1: 'to be agitated, to worry'; s.v. 'strut': 'to walk in an affected, pompous manner, as actors on a stage.'

sources.name: Muir, ed., Macbeth (Arden 2nd, 1951)
sources.citation: Muir, K., ed. Macbeth. Arden Shakespeare, 2nd series (1951), note to 5.5.19-28: the triple anaphora and the theatrical metaphor as Macbeth's nihilistic response to Lady Macbeth's death.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2181

OED s.v. 'player' n.3a and Schmidt are genuine lexicographic sources; the Muir Arden Second Series edition is confirmed as first published 1951, and the cited note (5.5.19-28 covering the triple anaphora and theatrical metaphor) is a plausible and standard scholarly locus for this passage.
Anaphora, theatrical conceit, and nihilistic reading are all mainstream and well-supported; the de casibus reference is peripheral and does not distort the central interpretation.

anchor_text: begin / To doubt the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth
summary: Macbeth realizes the witches' prophecy was a trick of language: the Third Apparition said he would never be conquered until Birnam Wood came to Dunsinane, which he took as impossible — but the words meant exactly what they said. 'Equivocation' was a notorious term in 1606: at the trial of the Jesuit Henry Garnet for the Gunpowder Plot, Garnet defended giving technically true but deliberately misleading answers under oath. The Porter had joked of 'an equivocator' going to hell (2.3). Here Macbeth names the witches' method — prophecies true in the letter and false in the spirit.
detail: Henry Garnet's 'Treatise of Equivocation' was produced as evidence at his trial (March 1606), the same year most scholars date Macbeth. The technique permitted a Catholic to swear 'I did not do X' while privately adding 'in this time and place' — technically not lying, but deliberately misleading. The play maps this onto the witches: 'none of woman born shall harm Macbeth' is literally true (Macduff was 'from his mother's womb untimely ripp'd'), and 'Birnam Wood shall never come to Dunsinane' is literally true (the wood does not move — soldiers carry its branches). Both statements 'lie like truth.' For an audience that had just watched a Jesuit hanged for equivocating about a plot to blow up the king, the word carried electric contemporary charge.

sources.name: The trial of Henry Garnet (1606)
sources.citation: The trial and execution of the Jesuit Henry Garnet, 3 May 1606, for complicity in the Gunpowder Plot; his defence of equivocation (mental reservation) became notorious. 'A Treatise of Equivocation' (MS attributed to Garnet, c. 1595) was produced against him.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2207

Garnet's trial conviction (28 March 1606), execution (3 May 1606), and the Treatise of Equivocation are all historically confirmed; the annotation's 'c. 1595' date for the Treatise MS is slightly earlier than the more commonly cited c. 1598 but within the plausible scholarly range and does not constitute fabrication; all substantive claims about equivocation doctrine and its mapping onto the witches are well-supported.

The Garnet/Gunpowder Plot equivocation connection is the standard historicist reading accepted by virtually all modern editors, and the two textual examples of witches' equivocating are both accurate.

anchor_text: die with harness on our back
summary: 'Harness' is a soldier's full armour — the complete set of plates covering the body. To die with harness on one's back means to die fighting in the field, in full armour, rather than in bed or in retreat. It is Macbeth's final, defiant resolution: whatever the prophecy means, he will not surrender or flee; he will go down as a soldier.

Compare Macbeth 5.3.51-52: 'Pull't off, I say. — What rhubarb, senna, or what purgative drug, / Would scour these English hence?' (Seyton arms Macbeth in the same scene cluster.)

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2217

OED s.v. 'harness' n.2 ('armour for man or horse; the complete equipment of a man-at-arms') and Onions Shakespeare Glossary are real, standard references that directly support the claim that 'harness' means full armour.
'Harness' as armour is uncontested, and the defiant dying-in-arms reading is the plain meaning of the line with no over-reach.

anchor_text: your leafy screens throw down
summary: Malcolm orders his troops to drop the branches they have been carrying as camouflage. This fulfills the witches' prophecy that Macbeth would be safe 'until Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill shall come against him' (4.1): the advancing army, each soldier hidden behind a bough cut from Birnam Wood, made the forest appear to move. Holinshed's Chronicles, Shakespeare's source, describes soldiers ordered to carry 'boughs cut from the trees' to conceal their numbers.
detail: The Birnam Wood prophecy was designed to seem impossible — a forest cannot march — so Macbeth took it as a guarantee of safety. Malcolm's tactic of using woodland camouflage is historically attested in Holinshed (Chronicles, 1587, 'History of Scotland'), though the dramatic irony belongs to Shakespeare's shaping of the material: the audience, having heard the prophecy in 4.1, knows exactly what Malcolm's boughs mean even before Macbeth does. The moment when a messenger tells Macbeth the wood is moving (5.5) is the hinge on which his confidence collapses. The 'leafy screens' serve a double function in performance: they are the literal camouflage of a pre-gunpowder ambush tactic, and the visible, onstage proof that equivocal prophecy is catching up with Macbeth.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd edition (1587), 'History of Scotland,' on Malcolm's campaign against Macbeth.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2218

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) 'History of Scotland' does describe Malcolm ordering his men to cut boughs at Birnam Wood as camouflage before the assault on Dunsinane; the source is real and directly supports both the historical-attestation claim and the prophecy-fulfilment context.
The Birnam Wood prophecy fulfillment, Holinshed sourcing, and the reading of 'leafy screens' as camouflage boughs are all mainstream and well-supported by the text at TLN 2218.

anchor_text: Lead our first battle
summary: 'Battle' here does not mean the whole engagement but a tactical unit of soldiers — what we would call a division or brigade. Malcolm assigns Siward and his son to command the leading division of the army, while Malcolm and Macduff take charge of whatever the plan requires beyond that. This sense of 'battle' as a body of troops was standard in Elizabethan military writing.

sources.name: OED s.v. battle
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'battle,' n., sense 8: 'A body of troops drawn up in fighting order; a division or squadron of an army.' Cf. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'battle.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2221

OED does record 'battle' in the sense of a body of troops or division of an army (an obsolete military sense), and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary covers the same; both cited works are real standard references that support the archaic-vocab claim.
'Battle' as a tactical division or squadron of troops is a well-attested Elizabethan military sense and fits Malcolm's assignment of Siward and his son to lead the vanguard.

anchor_text: Do we but find the tyrant's power to-night
summary: 'Power' here means armed force or army, not personal authority. Siward is saying: if we can only bring Macbeth's forces to battle tonight, let us be beaten if we cannot fight — a soldier's blunt expression of confidence. The construction 'Do we but...' is an archaic conditional meaning 'if we only...'; modern English would say 'If we can just find his army tonight.'

sources.name: OED s.v. power
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'power,' n., sense 11a: 'A military force; an army.' Cf. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'power.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2225

OED records 'power' in the sense of 'a military force; an army' as a historical usage attested from c. 1300 and common in Shakespeare; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference that also documents this sense, so the cited sources support the claim.
'Power' meaning army or armed force is a standard Elizabethan usage, and the gloss on 'Do we but' as a conditional meaning 'if we only' correctly reads Siward's soldier's confidence.

anchor_text: tied me to a stake; I cannot fly
summary: Bear-baiting was a popular Elizabethan blood sport in which a bear was chained ('tied') to a post and set upon by dogs; the bear could not flee and had to fight until it or the dogs were killed. Macbeth uses the image to describe his own position at Dunsinane — cornered, unable to run, forced to stand and fight.
detail: Arenas for bear-baiting stood near the Globe Theatre on the Southside of the Thames; audiences who attended Shakespeare's plays would have recognized the image instantly. The word 'course' in the next line is also bear-baiting vocabulary: a 'course' was one sustained attack by the dogs on the bear. The passage makes Macbeth simultaneously pitiable (like a baited bear) and defiant — he cannot fly, but he can still fight. His only remaining 'out' is the witches' prophecy that 'none of woman born' can harm him, which he clings to in the next lines and which Macduff will shortly destroy.

sources.name: OED s.v. 'course'
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'course,' n. sense 14b: a bout or run in bear-baiting or bull-baiting.

sources.name: Gurr, The Shakespearean Stage
sources.citation: Andrew Gurr, The Shakespearean Stage 1574-1642, 4th ed. (Cambridge UP, 2009), pp. 17-19 (the Bankside bear-garden and its proximity to the Globe).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2229

OED 'course' n. sense for bear-baiting bouts is well-attested, and Gurr's Shakespearean Stage 4th ed. (Cambridge UP, 2009) is a real and standard reference covering the Bankside bear-garden's proximity to the Globe.
The bear-baiting image is fully supported by the text ('tied to a stake,' 'bear-like,' 'course') and the Bankside proximity gloss is standard theatrical history; no overreach.

anchor_text: swords I smile at, weapons laugh to scorn
summary: Macbeth's confidence comes entirely from the second apparition's prophecy (4.1) that 'none of woman born / shall harm Macbeth.' He believes this protects him from every enemy — so he literally laughs at swords. The scene will shortly destroy this certainty: Macduff was delivered by what we would now call a caesarean section, not born 'of woman' in the conventional sense, and is therefore the one person the prophecy never covered.
detail: The witches' promise is an example of what the play calls 'equivocation' — technically true statements that lead their hearer to a false conclusion. Macbeth hears 'none of woman born shall harm me' and concludes he is invulnerable; the prophecy is literally fulfilled when Macduff, 'from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd' (5.8), kills him. The Jesuit doctrine of equivocation was a contemporary scandal: at the 1606 trial of Henry Garnet (a conspirator in the 1605 Gunpowder Plot), the defendant defended deliberately misleading answers under oath. Macbeth curses 'the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth' just two scenes earlier (5.5). His contemptuous 'weapons laugh to scorn' measures how completely the witches have misled him.

sources.name: The trial of Henry Garnet (1606)
sources.citation: The trial and execution of the Jesuit Henry Garnet, March 1606, for complicity in the Gunpowder Plot and his defence of equivocation (mental reservation); widely reported in contemporary accounts.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), History of Scotland: the three witches' prophecy to Macbeth that none of woman born can harm him.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2244

Garnet trial date (28 March 1606) and equivocation defense are historically accurate; Holinshed's Chronicles does contain the Macduff untimely-ripped passage that underlies the 'none of woman born' prophecy, making both citations legitimate support for the claims.

The equivocation/Garnet link is mainstream scholarship for this play, the prophecy mechanics are accurately described, and the reading of Macbeth's contempt as self-deceived confidence is defensible and widely held.

anchor_text: wretched kerns, whose arms / Are hired to bear their staves
summary: 'Kerns' were Irish or Scottish light infantry — lightly armored foot soldiers who fought with short spears or javelins. 'Staves' (plural of 'staff') means long wooden spear-shafts or poles. Macduff refuses to waste his sword on these low-ranking hired soldiers; he wants only Macbeth.
detail: In Elizabethan military usage, kerns (from Irish ceithearn) ranked below 'gallowglasses' — the heavier, better-armed infantry — and were often described in English writing as irregular, mercenary, and untrustworthy. The phrase 'hired to bear their staves' underlines that they have no personal stake in the fight: they carry their weapons for pay, not out of loyalty or principle. Macduff's contempt for them focuses his quest: killing ordinary soldiers would leave his sword 'undeeded' (TLN 2252) — unused for the one deed it exists to do.

Kerns as light-armed Irish/Scottish foot soldiers ranking below gallowglasses is correct Elizabethan military usage; 'hired to bear their staves' plainly supports the mercenary-contempt reading.

anchor_text: sword, with an unbatter'd edge, / I sheathe again undeeded
summary: 'Undeeded' means 'having performed no deed' — Macduff says that if he cannot find Macbeth himself, he will sheathe his sword without having done what it set out to do. The word captures his single-minded purpose: killing Macbeth is the one act his whole return from England has been aimed at, and any other killing would be beside the point.
detail: The coinage 'undeeded' is rare (OED cites this passage as the primary example). Its force comes from the parallel with 'unbatter'd edge': a sword with an untouched, still-sharp blade is literally undamaged, but also symbolically without purpose — it has done nothing. For Macduff, whose wife and children Macbeth had slaughtered (4.2), the 'deed' the sword owes is personal vengeance as well as political justice. The word belongs to a pattern of negative coinages in Macbeth — 'unreal,' 'unmann'd,' 'undivulged' — that mark things in a state of being not yet achieved or not yet revealed.

The gloss is accurate, the OED first-citation claim is defensible, and the pattern of negative-prefix coinages in Macbeth is a real, unremarkable critical observation with no overreach.

anchor_text: foes / That strike beside us
summary: 'Strike beside us' means 'strike to one side of us — that is, deliberately miss.' Malcolm notes that some of the enemy soldiers are throwing their fight, intentionally swinging wide rather than hitting Malcolm's men. This reflects Siward's preceding report that 'the tyrant's people on both sides do fight' — meaning some of Macbeth's own soldiers have turned coat and are now fighting for Malcolm.
detail: The syntax is compressed: 'foes that strike beside us' does not mean 'enemies fighting alongside us' but 'enemies who aim their blows off to the side of us' — i.e., fighting half-heartedly or defecting in practice if not yet in declaration. The desertion of Macbeth's forces is a recurring motif in Act 5: thanes and soldiers peel away from the tyrant throughout the act (Angus observes his title 'hang loose about him, like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief,' 5.2). By 5.7 the collapse is nearly complete: the castle has been surrendered 'gently' (TLN 2256), the thanes fight bravely for Malcolm, and Macbeth's remaining defenders are either mercenary kerns or reluctant soldiers who would rather miss than kill.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'beside'
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Robert D. Eagleson (Oxford UP, 1986), s.v. 'beside': 'aside, out of the right course'; compare 'beside the mark.'

Onions's gloss of 'beside' as 'aside, out of the right course' is standard lexicography, and Muir's Arden 2nd-series Macbeth (Methuen, 1951) is a confirmed real edition whose note at 5.7.28-29 gives the standard 'deliberately miss' reading.

The reading 'deliberately miss' is the mainstream Arden/Muir interpretation and is supported by Siward's preceding report that the tyrant's people fight on both sides, signaling defection; no overreach.

anchor_text: play the Roman fool, and die On mine own sword
summary: Macbeth refuses to kill himself rather than be captured. 'The Roman fool' is the Stoic Roman who fell on his own sword to escape defeat or dishonour — Cato at Utica (46 BCE) and Brutus at Philippi (42 BCE) being the famous examples. Macbeth rejects that code: while enemies are still alive, killing himself would be pointless waste.
detail: The Roman suicide-ideal held that a free man should choose death over captivity or the indignity of being led in a victor's triumph. Shakespeare had dramatized it in Julius Caesar and would return to it in Antony and Cleopatra. Here Macbeth frames self-slaughter as foolishness ('fool'), not honour: he turns the Stoic argument on its head — there are still lives to take. The speech establishes his final stance: he will fight to the last, not yield and not destroy himself.

sources.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Brutus 51-52 and Life of Cato the Younger 66-70 (North's 1579 translation); the Stoic Roman suicide at Utica and Philippi as the canonical models of honourable self-destruction.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2264

Plutarch's Life of Brutus (chapters 51-52 in North) and Life of Cato the Younger (chapters 66-70 in North) are genuine and describe the canonical Roman sword-suicides at Philippi and Utica that underpin the 'antique Roman' ideal; North's 1579 translation is the correct scholarly attribution for Shakespeare's source.
Macbeth's rejection of Stoic self-slaughter in favour of continued fighting is exactly what the text says, and Cato/Brutus as the canonical exemplars of the 'Roman fool' suicide is mainstream.

anchor_text: intrenchant air With thy keen sword impress
summary: 'Intrenchant' means incapable of being cut or wounded — not able to be trenched (sliced) by a blade. Macbeth is saying: trying to cut the air with a sword is as useless as trying to make him bleed, because he bears a charmed life that cannot be ended by anyone 'of woman born.' 'Impress' here means to make a mark or wound.
detail: 'Intrenchant' (also spelled 'intrinchant' in some early texts) is a nonce-formation from the verb 'trench' (to cut). The OED cites this passage as one of the earliest usages. The image of striking unresisting air to make a point about futility is a deliberate taunt: Macbeth invites Macduff to waste his effort on something literally impossible before reminding him of the prophecy. 'Impress' in the sense of leaving a mark on — to impress a seal in wax — is the sense in play, not the military 'press' (conscript).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'intrenchant' (adj.): 'That cannot be cut; not subject to incision,' first attested in this passage.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'intrenchant': glossed as 'that cannot be cut, incapable of receiving a wound.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2275

OED s.v. 'intrenchant' citing this Macbeth passage as the earliest attestation is a standard lexicographic fact, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon carries the gloss as cited; both sources genuinely support the archaic-vocab claim.
'Intrenchant' as 'incapable of being cut' and 'impress' as 'make a mark/wound' are the standard glosses, and the image of fruitlessly striking the air as a taunt is an unforced reading of the line.

anchor_text: Despair thy charm; And let the angel whom thou still hast serv'd Tell thee, Macduff was from his mother's womb Untimely ripp'd
summary: 'Despair thy charm' means 'give up your trust in the witches' prophecy.' 'The angel thou still hast serv'd' is a bitter irony — Macduff is naming the devil (a fallen angel) whom Macbeth has served throughout the play. 'Untimely ripp'd' means delivered by caesarean section before full term, so Macduff was not technically 'born of woman' in the ordinary way — exploiting the exact loophole in the Second Apparition's prophecy.
detail: In early modern understanding, a child delivered surgically after the mother's death or by emergency operation was not said to have been 'born' of a woman in the same sense as a child delivered naturally. The Second Apparition (4.1) had said 'none of woman born shall harm Macbeth' — true, but equivocal, because Macduff's delivery was not a natural birth. This is the witches' ultimate equivocation: the prophecy was literally true, and fatally misleading. The word 'angel' for a devil-servant is acutely sarcastic, given Macbeth's career of murder; 'still' means 'always' (up to this moment).

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of Scotland: the prophecy that none 'of woman borne' could harm Macbeth, and the revelation that Macduff was 'ripped out of his mother's womb' rather than born naturally.

Reading 'the angel thou still hast serv'd' as bitter irony for the devil, and 'untimely ripp'd' as the witches' equivocation exploiting caesarean delivery to fulfil the prophecy literally, are both mainstream and well-supported by the text.

anchor_text: juggling fiends no more believ'd, That palter with us in a double sense
summary: 'Juggling' means cheating or deceiving — not the modern sense of tossing objects, but the older sense of trickery (a 'juggler' was a conjurer-fraud). 'Palter' means to deal deceitfully or use words in an evasive, misleading way. Macbeth realises the witches gave him prophecies that were technically true but designed to destroy him: he heard what he wanted to hear, and the fiends knew it.
detail: The speech names the play's deepest theme: equivocation. The witches' promises were not lies but truths framed to mislead — 'none of woman born,' 'till Birnam wood / Do come to Dunsinane.' Both came true in unexpected ways. 'Palter in a double sense' echoes the Elizabethan doctrine of equivocation debated at the trial of the Jesuit Henry Garnet in 1606, the year the play was likely written; for Shakespeare's audience, 'equivocators' who 'lied like truth' were a live and frightening idea. Macbeth connects the fiends' method to the political crime of the moment.

sources.name: The trial of Henry Garnet (1606)
sources.citation: The trial and execution of the Jesuit Henry Garnet, March 1606, for his part in the Gunpowder Plot and his defence of equivocation (mental reservation); widely reported and debated in the year Macbeth was composed.

Henry Garnet's trial (conviction 28 March 1606, execution 3 May 1606) and his public defence of equivocation are historically confirmed and are the standard scholarly context for this passage; OED entries for 'palter' and 'juggling' are real and supportive.
'Juggling' as conjurer-fraud, 'palter' as equivocate, and the connection to the Garnet trial and Elizabethan equivocation doctrine are all standard scholarly readings for this passage.

anchor_text: Your son, my lord, has paid a soldier's debt: He only liv'd but till he was a man
summary: Ross's phrase 'paid a soldier's debt' is a formal Elizabethan expression meaning he fulfilled his duty by dying in battle — a soldier 'owes' his life to his country and his lord, and death in action is the payment. The lines that follow underline the idea: Young Siward lived just long enough to prove himself a man, and then died like one. Siward's stoic response ('Then he is dead?' / 'God's soldier be he') is the soldier's code: a good death facing the enemy is enough.
detail: The exchange between Ross and Siward dramatizes the Elizabethan soldier's ethic of honour-in-death. Siward's only question is whether his son's wounds were on the front of his body — meaning he faced his enemy and did not flee. 'Had he his hurts before?' (TLN 2316) confirms that Young Siward died in action, not running away, which closes the account: 'God's soldier be he.' The scene gives the English general dignity alongside Macduff's triumph, and briefly humanizes the faceless battle deaths the play has been accumulating since Act 5 began.
