Holinshed's 1587 Chronicles does record Siward's son being killed in the Scottish campaign against Macbeth, and Schmidt s.v. 'debt' is a legitimate lexicographic source for the phrase 'pay a debt'; both sources support the claim.
'Paid a soldier's debt' as dying in battle to fulfil the obligation of military service, with honour confirmed by wounds on the front, is the straightforward and mainstream reading of this exchange.

anchor_text: My thanes and kinsmen, Henceforth be earls, the first that ever Scotland In such an honour nam'd
summary: Malcolm converts the Scottish title 'thane' into the English title 'earl.' A thane was a Scottish nobleman — Macbeth himself was Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor. An earl was the equivalent English rank. By adopting English titles Malcolm signals the end of the old, Macbeth-era order and a political realignment with England, which had supplied the army that restored his throne.
detail: Shakespeare found this detail in Holinshed, who records that Malcolm III, on his return from England, replaced the Scottish thanedoms with English earldoms — a change that reflected the English support for his accession and began the gradual anglicisation of the Scottish nobility. For a Jacobean audience under James I, who united the crowns of Scotland and England in 1603, the moment carried a pointed resonance: the play's final gesture is a Scotland aligning itself with English institutions, the origin story of the union James embodied. The word 'thane' had appeared throughout the play as the marker of Scottish identity; its replacement here is both political and symbolic.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of Scotland: Malcolm III's conversion of Scottish thaneships into English-style earldoms after his accession.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2336

Holinshed's 1587 Chronicles records Malcolm creating the first Scottish earldoms (Fife, Menteth, Atholl, etc.) after his accession, which directly supports Shakespeare's dramatic moment of Malcolm converting thanes to earls.

Malcolm's conversion of Scottish thanedoms to English earldoms, sourced to Holinshed and read as a Jacobean union resonance for James I's audience, is a well-established scholarly interpretation with textual grounding.

anchor_text: by self and violent hands Took off her life
summary: 'Took off her life' is a formal euphemism for killing. 'Self and violent hands' means hands turned violently against herself — suicide. Malcolm reports that Lady Macbeth apparently died by her own hand, though even here ('as 'tis thought') the play withholds certainty. This is the play's only direct reference to her death; the audience already heard the offstage cry and Seyton's bare announcement ('The queen, my lord, is dead,' 5.5) but was given no detail.
detail: The phrase 'lay violent hands upon oneself' was a standard Elizabethan legal and religious formula for suicide. Suicide was a crime as well as a sin: a self-murderer (felo de se) forfeited property to the Crown and, unless the jury found lunacy, was denied Christian burial — the dilemma that haunts the gravedigger's argument about Ophelia in Hamlet. Malcolm's 'as 'tis thought' is careful: it may reflect genuine uncertainty, or diplomatic restraint in victory, or the play's habitual tactic of not spelling out the worst. The detail is consistent with Lady Macbeth's deterioration in 5.1 and the Doctor's prognosis that she needs 'the divine rather than the physician.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'violent' (in the reflexive sense, turned against oneself) and 'take off' (= to kill, put to death).

sources.name: Tudor-Stuart law on self-murder
sources.citation: On 'self and violent hands' as the period's legal-religious formula for suicide (felo de se): the self-murderer forfeited goods to the Crown and, absent a verdict of lunacy, was denied Christian burial (cf. the coroner's-quest debate over Ophelia, Hamlet 5.1).
